title: AUD U2·W2 — Audit Sampling (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — testing a slice of the whole

The auditor cannot examine every one of MBG's thousands of transactions, so it tests a sample and projects the result to the population. Audit sampling is applying a procedure to less than 100% of a population such that every item could be selected, to draw a conclusion about the whole. The discipline is managing the risk that the sample misleads — the subject of this heavily tested week.

Sampling risk versus nonsampling risk

Two risks attend a sample. Sampling risk is the risk that the sample is not representative, so a conclusion drawn from it differs from the conclusion the auditor would reach by testing the whole population — it is inherent to sampling and is controlled by sample size. Nonsampling risk is the risk of a wrong conclusion for any other reason — using an inappropriate procedure, misinterpreting evidence, or failing to recognize a misstatement — and is controlled by training, supervision, and review, not sample size.

Attribute sampling for tests of controls

Attribute sampling tests a rate of occurrence — how often a control fails (a deviation) — to decide whether to rely on the control. Sample size grows with the expected deviation rate and the desired confidence, and shrinks as the tolerable deviation rate (the maximum failure rate the auditor will accept and still rely) rises. Note that population size has little effect on sample size for a large population — a counterintuitive but tested point.

Evaluating a controls sample

After testing, the auditor computes the sample deviation rate (deviations ÷ sample size) and adds an allowance for sampling risk to get the upper deviation rate. If the upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable rate, the auditor may rely on the control as planned; if it exceeds tolerable, the auditor cannot rely and must increase substantive testing. Worked example: with a tolerable deviation rate of 7%, a sample of 60 yields 2 deviations — a 3.3% sample rate; if the resulting upper deviation rate (say 6.5%) stays at or below 7%, reliance is supported.

Sampling risks in tests of controls

Two sampling risks have opposite consequences. The risk of assessing control risk too low (overreliance) is the danger that the sample suggests a control works when it does not — this relates to effectiveness and is the more serious risk, because it leads the auditor to do too little substantive work. The risk of assessing control risk too high (underreliance) suggests a good control is bad — a problem of efficiency, leading to unnecessary testing. Auditors guard most carefully against the effectiveness risk.

Substantive sampling and monetary-unit sampling

For substantive tests the auditor samples dollar amounts, not occurrence rates. Monetary-unit sampling (MUS), also called probability-proportional-to-size, treats each dollar as a sampling unit, so larger balances are automatically more likely to be selected — efficient when the auditor expects few misstatements and is testing for overstatement (it is the standard tool for receivables). MUS projects a most likely misstatement plus an allowance to an upper misstatement limit, compared against tolerable misstatement. A weakness: MUS handles understatement and zero/negative balances poorly.

Classical variables sampling

Classical variables sampling uses statistical estimation of an amount rather than a rate, with methods like mean-per-unit, ratio, and difference estimation. It is better suited than MUS when the auditor expects a larger number of misstatements or is concerned with understatement (testing completeness, such as searching for unrecorded liabilities). The trade-off is that it requires an estimate of the population's standard deviation and is more complex, but it gives a two-sided estimate MUS cannot.

Sampling risks in substantive tests

Substantive sampling has its own paired risks. The risk of incorrect acceptance is concluding a materially misstated balance is fairly stated — an effectiveness risk that, like overreliance, undermines the audit and is guarded against most. The risk of incorrect rejection is concluding a fairly stated balance is misstated — an efficiency problem that causes wasted work (extended testing that eventually clears the balance). Sample size rises as the auditor seeks to lower incorrect acceptance, as tolerable misstatement falls, and as expected misstatement rises.

Selecting the sample

How items are chosen affects whether a sample is representative. Random selection gives every item an equal chance; systematic selection takes every nth item after a random start (efficient, but risky if the population follows a pattern); monetary-unit selection picks dollars (favoring large balances); and haphazard selection is a non-statistical attempt at randomness without conscious bias. Block selection — choosing contiguous items — is generally inappropriate, because a block is unlikely to represent the population. Statistical sampling lets the auditor measure sampling risk; nonstatistical sampling relies on judgment; both are permitted if properly designed.

Factors that drive sample size

The exam rewards knowing how each factor moves sample size. For tests of controls, sample size increases with higher desired confidence and a higher expected deviation rate, and decreases as the tolerable deviation rate rises. For substantive tests, sample size increases as the assessed risk of material misstatement rises, as the desired assurance grows (a lower acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance), and as expected misstatement increases, and it decreases as tolerable misstatement rises. A dual-purpose test uses one sample to both test a control and substantiate the related transactions, sized as the larger of the two requirements. Population size, again, has a negligible effect once the population is large.

Projecting and concluding

Whatever the method, the auditor projects the sample result to the population and compares it to the relevant limit. In attribute sampling the projected (upper) deviation rate is compared to the tolerable deviation rate; in substantive sampling the projected misstatement plus an allowance for sampling risk is compared to tolerable misstatement. If the projection exceeds the limit, the auditor responds — expanding the sample, performing alternative procedures, or proposing an adjustment — and never simply accepts a result that breaches tolerance. The discipline is the same across methods: estimate, add a margin for sampling risk, and conclude against a pre-set threshold.

CMA bridge

Sampling is the statistical backbone behind the substantive procedures and tests of controls from AUD Unit 1. The risk-of-incorrect-acceptance and overreliance risks are the sampling expression of the audit-risk model — both are about wrongly concluding things are fine when they are not, the core danger the whole audit is built to avoid.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish sampling risk (controlled by sample size) from nonsampling risk (controlled by supervision and review).
  2. Use attribute sampling for controls: compare the upper deviation rate to the tolerable deviation rate; population size barely affects sample size.
  3. Use MUS for overstatement with few expected misstatements; use classical variables when more misstatements or understatement is the concern.
  4. Guard most against the effectiveness risks — assessing control risk too low (overreliance) and incorrect acceptance — over the efficiency risks.

Recap: sampling risk is the chance an unrepresentative sample misleads, managed by sample size, while nonsampling risk is managed by review; attribute sampling relies on a control only when the upper deviation rate stays at or below tolerable; MUS targets overstatement of larger balances while classical variables sampling handles understatement and more misstatements; and the auditor most fears the effectiveness errors — overreliance and incorrect acceptance — that make a flawed balance look fine.

flashcards.back: Sampling risk = the sample is unrepresentative (controlled by sample size); nonsampling risk = wrong conclusion for any other reason (controlled by training/supervision/review).

flashcards.front: Tolerable deviation rate effect on sample size
flashcards.back: A higher tolerable deviation rate lowers required sample size; population size has little effect for large populations.

flashcards.front: Relying on a control from a sample
flashcards.back: Rely if the upper deviation rate (sample rate + allowance for sampling risk) is at or below the tolerable deviation rate.

flashcards.front: Risk of assessing control risk too LOW
flashcards.back: Overreliance — concluding a control works when it doesn't; an EFFECTIVENESS risk (most serious), leading to too little substantive testing.

flashcards.front: Risk of incorrect acceptance vs rejection
flashcards.back: Incorrect acceptance = a misstated balance looks fair (effectiveness, most serious); incorrect rejection = a fair balance looks misstated (efficiency, wasted work).

questions.q: Sampling risk is controlled primarily by:
questions.explain: Sampling risk (an unrepresentative sample) is managed by sample size; nonsampling risk is managed by supervision/review.

questions.q: Attribute sampling is used to test:
choices: The rate of deviation in a control
The dollar amount of a balance
questions.explain: Attribute sampling tests a rate of occurrence — typically control deviations.

questions.q: An auditor may rely on a control when the:
choices: Upper deviation rate is at or below the tolerable deviation rate
Sample deviation rate is zero only
questions.explain: Reliance is supported when the upper deviation rate does not exceed the tolerable rate.

questions.q: The risk of assessing control risk too LOW (overreliance) primarily affects audit:
questions.explain: Overreliance leads to too little substantive testing — an effectiveness (and the more serious) risk.

questions.q: Monetary-unit sampling is MOST efficient when the auditor:
choices: Expects few misstatements and tests for overstatement
questions.explain: MUS suits few-expected-misstatement, overstatement testing (e.g., receivables); it is weak for understatement and zero balances.

questions.q: Classical variables sampling is preferable to MUS when:
choices: A larger number of misstatements or understatement is expected
questions.explain: Classical variables sampling handles more misstatements and understatement (completeness) better than MUS.

questions.q: The risk of incorrect acceptance is the risk that:
choices: A materially misstated balance is concluded to be fairly stated
A fairly stated balance is rejected
questions.explain: Incorrect acceptance — a misstated balance looks fair — is the effectiveness risk the auditor guards against most.
